Studies have shown that the severity of insulin resistance exerts a significant and independent negative effect on myocardial mechanical efficiency, even in non-diabetic individuals, highlighting the potential role of IR in cardiovascular disease, especially among populations without diabetes. Regardless of diabetic status, IR and its accompanying metabolic disturbances can promote the onset and progression of CHD [ ]. Individuals with IR are more prone to hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and hypertension, all of which are closely associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes [ ]. Therefore, IR is not only regarded as a potential pathophysiological mechanism of cardiovascular disease but also serves as an important marker for cardiovascular risk assessment. Furthermore, IR plays a particularly critical role in metabolic syndrome, being strongly associated with obesity, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, and low levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol [ , ]. Notably, these metabolic abnormalities have been confirmed as independent risk factors for cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ – ], further underscoring the pivotal role of IR in the development and progression of CVD. Due to the complexity and high cost of traditional IR assessment methods, researchers have proposed the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index as a convenient and cost-effective surrogate marker [ , ]. The TyG index does not rely on insulin measurements and is applicable to a wide range of populations, offering significant clinical value for metabolic health assessment and cardiovascular risk prediction [ ]. In individuals with normal glucose metabolism, activation of insulin receptors triggers signaling to IRS-1 (insulin receptor substrate-1), which then interacts with and activates the downstream PI3-kinase (PI3K, a p85/p110 complex). This leads to activation of Akt, promoting the translocation of GLUT4 to the cell membrane and facilitating glucose uptake into cells for metabolism. Additionally, this pathway activates nitric oxide synthase (NOS), promoting vasodilation and maintaining endothelial function. In patients with hyperglycemia, impaired IRS-1 signaling results in reduced glucose metabolism and decreased eNOS activity, thereby impairing vasodilation. Meanwhile, the MAP kinase pathway remains sensitive to insulin. The insulin resistance of the IRS-1/PI3K pathway leads to compensatory hyperinsulinemia, which in turn excessively activates the MAPK pathway, promoting inflammation, cellular proliferation, and the progression of atherosclerosis. Dyslipidemia contributes to this process by triggering inflammatory storms mediated by NF-κB and inhibiting IRS-1 function, thus forming a vicious cycle between insulin resistance and atherosclerosis. As an integrated marker of glucose and lipid metabolism, the TyG index reflects the metabolic burden resulting from the combined dysregulation of triglycerides and fasting glucose. Compared to individual metabolic parameters, the TyG index more sensitively captures abnormal signals arising from the interaction between glucose and lipid metabolism. In recent years, studies have suggested that dynamic monitoring of biomarkers offers substantial advantages over single time-point measurements. Considering that triglyceride and fasting glucose levels may fluctuate over time, potentially leading to regression dilution bias, this study identified three distinct TyG trajectories in acute STEMI patients following PCI, based on serial TyG values: the persistently high group (trajectory 1), the moderate-level group (trajectory 2), and the rapid decline group (trajectory 3). The incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) differed significantly among the three groups ( P < 0.05). Compared with the persistently high group, the rapid decline group exhibited significantly lower rates of ischemia-driven target vessel revascularization, heart failure rehospitalization, nonfatal acute myocardial infarction, cardiac death, and total MACE events (all P < 0.05). Survival analysis demonstrated that the prognostic endpoints significantly differed among the groups, as indicated by the survival curves (P for log-rank < 0.001). To further explore the prognostic impact of different metabolic trajectories within various clinical subgroups, a subgroup analysis was performed. The persistently high group exhibited a consistently higher risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) across most subgroups, with statistically significant differences compared to the rapid decline group. This association was particularly pronounced among patients with multivessel disease and those classified as Killip class III–IV, suggesting that metabolic trajectories hold important prognostic value, especially for risk stratification in high-risk patients. Furthermore, multivariate Cox regression analysis, after adjusting for confounding variables including sex, age, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, uric acid, body mass index (BMI), hypertension, diabetes mellitus, family history of coronary heart disease, smoking history, multivessel disease, ejection fraction, Killip classification, as well as baseline and final TyG values, confirmed that the trajectory grouping remained an independent prognostic factor ( P < 0.05). These findings indicate that the predictive value of TyG trajectories for long-term prognosis in STEMI patients remains robust across different adjustment models, highlighting its independent prognostic significance. In addition to STEMI, the TyG index has also been reported as a valuable risk predictor in various cardiovascular diseases, including hypertension, heart failure, and atherosclerosis. Existing evidence preliminarily supports the potential of the TyG index as a metabolic biomarker for clinical risk assessment. In the following section, we will systematically summarize the current research progress on the TyG index across different cardiovascular diseases. TyG index and hypertension: from risk prediction to target organ damage and clinical outcomes In a longitudinal study of hypertension involving 4,600 Chinese adults, analysis showed that for each 1.0-unit increase in the TyG index, the risk of developing new-onset hypertension increased by 17%. Long-term follow-up further identified three distinct TyG index trajectories: the “low-level rising group,” the “moderate-level rising group,” and the “high-level stable group.” Compared with the “low-level rising group,” the risk of hypertension was significantly higher in the other two groups (HR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.23–1.54; HR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.40–2.02), with the risk being particularly pronounced in the female subgroup (HR = 2.63 and 4.66) [ ]. Moreover, coronary heart disease patients with concomitant hypertension and elevated TyG index showed a 47% increased risk of MACE within one year [ , ]. The TyG index is also significantly associated with the incidence of albuminuria, vascular injury, and cardiac remodeling in hypertensive patients. Patients with higher TyG index levels were found to have significantly increased left atrial volume index and left ventricular mass index, along with reduced E′ velocity and E/A ratio ( P < 0.05). Multivariate regression analysis further confirmed that this association was independent of other risk factors ( P < 0.001) [ , ]. A retrospective study involving 4,710 patients demonstrated that individuals with persistently elevated and poorly controlled TyG index levels had a significantly increased risk of stroke (OR = 2.161, 95% CI: 1.446–3.228) [ ]. The TyG index has been identified as an independent risk factor for stroke [ ], and in hypertensive patients, the risk of first-ever stroke increases with higher TyG index levels. This association was especially prominent among elderly individuals (HR = 2.15, 95% CI: 1.50–3.07, P < 0.001) [ ]. Further supporting evidence comes from a multicenter analysis conducted across 22 hospitals in Suzhou, which included 3,216 patients with acute ischemic stroke. The study revealed that a higher TyG index was closely associated with an increased risk of poor functional outcomes at discharge and higher in-hospital mortality, highlighting its potential value in short-term prognostic assessment [ ]. Additionally, a study involving 356 hospitalized patients showed that the TyG index was significantly higher in the atrial fibrillation group compared to the non-atrial fibrillation group, and the TyG index was identified as an independent risk factor for atrial fibrillation. Subgroup analysis revealed that the association between the TyG index and atrial fibrillation was more evident in non-diabetic patients, whereas this correlation was not observed in diabetic individuals [ ]. The relationship between TyG index and heart failure risk, and prognosis Beyond hypertension, the TyG index has also been shown to be closely associated with the incidence of heart failure. Analyses from the Kailuan prospective cohort, which included 95,996 participants, and a retrospective Hong Kong cohort involving 19,345 participants — with 2,726 and 1,709 heart failure cases identified respectively — demonstrated that the TyG index is an independent risk factor for heart failure [ , ]. Other studies have reported that a higher TyG index is significantly associated with increased risks of mortality and rehospitalization among patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), suggesting that the TyG index could serve as a promising prognostic marker for this patient population [ ]. In patients with acute decompensated heart failure, an elevated TyG index was significantly linked to an increased risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular death, and major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCEs). Particularly, patients with a TyG index ≥ 9.32 were at markedly higher risk for both mortality and MACCEs [ ]. Among patients with chronic heart failure, those with a higher TyG index also exhibited significantly increased risks of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. Specifically, patients with elevated TyG index had a 1.84-fold higher risk of all-cause death and a 1.94-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death compared to those with lower values. Moreover, incorporating the TyG index into existing risk prediction models significantly improved their predictive performance, further underscoring its critical role as a prognostic indicator for mortality in

Among patients with chronic heart failure, those with a higher TyG index also exhibited significantly increased risks of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. Specifically, patients with elevated TyG index had a 1.84-fold higher risk of all-cause death and a 1.94-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death compared to those with lower values. Moreover, incorporating the TyG index into existing risk prediction models significantly improved their predictive performance, further underscoring its critical role as a prognostic indicator for mortality in chronic heart failure patients [ – ]. The association between TyG index and arteriosclerosis Arteriosclerosis, an early manifestation of vascular aging, is characterized primarily by reduced arterial elasticity and elevated pulse pressure, and it is closely associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. A growing body of evidence has demonstrated a positive correlation between the TyG index and arteriosclerosis, as measured by parameters such as pulse wave velocity (PWV), and has suggested that the TyG index may outperform traditional insulin resistance measures like the HOMA-IR index in predicting arteriosclerosis. Lambrinoudaki et al. reported a positive association between the TyG index and brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (baPWV), although their study population was limited to postmenopausal women [ ]. Similarly, a Korean study confirmed an independent positive correlation between the TyG index and baPWV and showed that the TyG index was superior to HOMA-IR for predicting arteriosclerosis [ ]. Li et al. further demonstrated that this association was particularly pronounced in men [ ], whereas Nakagomi et al. found the correlation to be stronger in women [ ], suggesting that sex and age differences may influence this relationship. Additionally, Wu et al. confirmed that the TyG index was correlated with changes in baPWV among hypertensive patients, indicating a possible synergistic effect of insulin resistance and hypertension in promoting the development of arteriosclerosis [ , ]. Wang et al. reported, in a cohort of 3,185 patients with type 2 diabetes, that the TyG index was positively correlated with arteriosclerosis and again showed superior predictive value compared to HOMA-IR [ ]. Guo et al. further demonstrated that the TyG index was significantly and positively associated with the 10-year cardiovascular disease risk in patients with arteriosclerosis [ ]. These findings collectively highlight the potential of the TyG index as a predictive marker for arteriosclerosis and provide valuable guidance for clinical management. The clinical significance of the TyG index in predicting cardiovascular disease and All-Cause mortality The TyG index has shown significant value in predicting the development, severity, and prognosis of coronary artery disease (CAD). A meta-analysis including 12 cohort studies with 6,354,990 participants confirmed that higher TyG levels are associated with increased risks of CAD (moderate certainty), myocardial infarction, and cardiovascular disease (very low certainty). A linear relationship was observed between the TyG index and the risk of CAD and composite cardiovascular events, though further prospective studies are needed, especially in non-Asian populations [ ]. Additionally, an elevated TyG index is closely related to coronary lesion complexity (SYNTAX score > 22) in ACS patients, independent of diabetes status [ , ]. In a 10-year cohort of 6,095 non-diabetic subjects, higher TyG quartiles were linked to a significantly increased risk of CVD, CHD, and stroke, and the inclusion of the TyG index improved the predictive performance of traditional risk models [ ]. NHANES-based studies also revealed that the TyG index is positively associated with chest pain and nonlinearly linked to all-cause mortality, independent of chest pain status [ ]. Moreover, the TyG index outperformed other markers in predicting long-term mortality in non-diabetic STEMI patients, particularly when TyG ≥ 9.83 [ ]. The TyG index also correlates with coronary lesion severity, abdominal aortic calcification [ , ]. Furthermore, a large NHANES-based study (20,194 participants) demonstrated that the TyG index is nonlinearly associated with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, particularly in individuals under 65 years. Compared to HOMA-IR, the TyG index showed superior predictive power for mortality outcomes [ ]. The clinical value of the TyG index in predicting complications after PCI in coronary artery disease patients Studies based on the MIMIC-III database have suggested that the TyG index holds potential value for predicting complications following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) ([ ]. Several studies have demonstrated that the TyG index is associated with an increased risk of in-stent restenosis and repeated revascularization, and has been identified as an independent predictor of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with premature coronary artery disease. A study [ , ] conducted by Fuwai Hospital in 2017 investigated the relationship between the TyG index, repeated revascularization, and in-stent restenosis in patients with chronic coronary syndrome who underwent drug-eluting stent implantation. Several studies have demonstrated that the TyG index is associated with an increased risk of in-stent restenosis and repeated revascularization, and has been identified as an independent predictor of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with premature coronary artery disease. A study [ , ] conducted by Fuwai Hospital in 2017 investigated the relationship between the TyG index, repeated revascularization, and in-stent restenosis in patients with chronic coronary syndrome who underwent drug-eluting stent implantation. A total of 1,414 patients were consecutively enrolled and followed for a median of 60 months. During follow-up, 548 patients (38.76%) experienced at least one major endpoint event. The incidence of major endpoints increased progressively with higher TyG index levels. After adjusting for potential confounders, the TyG index remained independently associated with major adverse outcomes in patients with chronic coronary syndrome (HR: 1.191, 95% CI: 1.038–1.367, P = 0.013) ([ – ], These findings suggest that an elevated TyG index is associated with a higher risk of post-PCI complications, including repeated revascularization and in-stent restenosis. However, its incremental predictive value for major adverse events remains limited, highlighting the need for further multicenter and large-scale clinical studies to clarify the role of the TyG index in long-term risk stratification and prognostic management after PCI ([ , ]. As a surrogate marker of insulin resistance (IR), the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index is closely associated with the onset and progression of the aforementioned diseases. Accumulating evidence has shown that the TyG index serves as a reliable predictor for cardiovascular outcomes in various populations. Notably, several nomogram-based models incorporating the TyG index have demonstrated good predictive performance for MACEs in patients with HFpEF post-CABG, new-onset hypertension, STEMI undergoing PCI, and chronic coronary disease. These models consistently reported satisfactory C-index values (ranging from 0.73 to 0.82), improved net reclassification, and clinical utility via DCA, indicating the wide applicability of TyG in cardiovascular risk prediction I [ – ]. From a systemic pathological perspective, metabolic dysregulation caused by insulin resistance involves multiple tissues and signaling pathways. The underlying mechanisms mainly involve endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammatory responses, and oxidative stress. Under physiological conditions, insulin regulates blood flow and glucose metabolism by promoting nitric oxide (NO) production in vascular endothelial cells. However, in the IR state, NO synthesis is reduced, impairing vascular relaxation function [ ]. In addition, IR can induce the sustained release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and C-reactive protein (CRP), as well as reactive oxygen species (ROS). These processes mutually reinforce each other, forming a vicious cycle of “inflammation-oxidative stress,” which further aggravates endothelial injury [ , ]. Meanwhile, a persistently elevated TyG index may also disrupt insulin secretion, promote myocardial fibrosis and left ventricular hypertrophy, ultimately leading to cardiac dysfunction [ ]. These pathological changes not only impair myocardial structure and function but may also destabilize coronary plaques and increase the risk of thrombosis. Furthermore, studies have shown that IR and hyperinsulinemia can activate serum/glucocorticoid-regulated kinase 1 (SGK1) through multiple signaling pathways and stimulate aldosterone secretion, which in turn further activates SGK1. As a shared node in insulin and aldosterone signaling, SGK1 increases intracellular sodium ion concentration in vascular smooth muscle cells by activating sodium channels, while inhibiting nitric oxide synthase activity and reducing NO production. This cascade ultimately leads to increased vascular tone, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular stiffening [ ]. In addition, the TyG index may contribute to the development of coronary artery disease (CAD) through its roles in dyslipidemia, diabetes, and hypertension, highlighting its central role in metabolic syndrome [ , ]. From the perspective of molecular signaling pathways, hyperglycemia impairs the IRS-1/PI3K signaling pathway, reducing glucose metabolism and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) activity, thereby contributing to endothelial dysfunction. Concurrently, hyperinsulinemia abnormally activates the MAPK pathway, promoting inflammation and vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, which accelerates atherosclerosis. Lipid dysregulation further aggravates insulin resistance via NF-κB–mediated inflammatory cascades and inhibition of IRS-1 signaling, creating a vicious cycle in the progression of atherosclerosis. As a composite indicator reflecting the metabolic burden of both glucose and lipid dysregulation, the TyG index may more sensitively capture these interactive abnormalities and underlying metabolic stress. Although no significant differences in FBG and TG levels were observed among groups in this study, the observed differences in TyG index suggest that it may better represent the overall metabolic risk and possess independent prognostic value. Based on the above mechanistic analysis, this study found that the group with a rapidly decreasing TyG index exhibited the lowest incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). This finding may be attributed to improved insulin sensitivity, reduced inflammatory levels, and restored coronary circulation function. Although no significant differences in FBG and TG levels were observed among groups in this study, the observed differences in TyG index suggest that it may better represent the overall metabolic risk and possess independent prognostic value. Based on the above mechanistic analysis, this study found that the group with a rapidly decreasing TyG index exhibited the lowest incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). This finding may be attributed to improved insulin sensitivity, reduced inflammatory levels, and restored coronary circulation function. Future research could further explore whether lifestyle interventions (such as low-carbohydrate diets and exercise training) or pharmacological therapies (such as sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 [SGLT2] inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 [GLP-1] receptor agonists) can improve the TyG index and thereby reduce the long-term cardiovascular risk in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The results of this study suggest that the TyG index trajectory holds significant clinical value in risk assessment for patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Trajectory-based monitoring of the TyG index can provide a more accurate prediction of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and assist in formulating more proactive metabolic management and cardiovascular protection strategies. These findings indicate that a single measurement of the TyG index is insufficient for comprehensive risk assessment, and regular monitoring of its trajectory may improve the accuracy of prognosis prediction. Future studies could explore the incorporation of the TyG trajectory into existing STEMI risk assessment models and evaluate the effectiveness of targeted interventions. Overall, as a simple and effective metabolic biomarker, the TyG index demonstrates considerable value for the early identification and personalized management of cardiovascular disease. Limitations and future perspectives This study revealed an association between TyG index trajectories and long-term prognosis in patients with STEMI; however, several limitations should be acknowledged: Study design and generalizability This study employed a single-center retrospective design, which limits the generalizability of the findings and may introduce selection bias. Nevertheless, the inclusion of 1,092 patients provides a relatively large sample size with considerable representativeness, enhancing the robustness of the conclusions. Lack of detailed medication information and potential confounding Information on glucose-lowering medication use was not collected. As such treatments can affect fasting glucose levels and indirectly influence the TyG index, the absence of these data may introduce unmeasured confounding. Moreover, the definition of “regular medication use” was based on patient self-reporting, and the retrospective nature of data collection may have led to bias in assessing medication adherence. Future prospective studies should collect detailed medication data to explore the impact of antidiabetic therapy on TyG trajectories and cardiovascular outcomes. Inclusion of patients with specific metabolic disorders This study did not exclude patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia or familial chylomicronemia syndrome, which may affect the accuracy of the TyG index in cardiovascular risk assessment. Although elevated triglyceride levels in these patients are typically related to acute pancreatitis rather than atherosclerosis, their specific impact on cardiovascular risk prediction remains unclear. Future studies should consider excluding or separately analyzing these patients to improve the applicability and predictive performance of the TyG index in diverse populations. Limited dynamic monitoring during the acute phase During hospitalization for acute myocardial infarction, triglyceride and fasting glucose levels are typically measured only at admission and at limited time points, lacking close monitoring of dynamic changes during the acute phase. This limitation mainly arises from routine clinical diagnostic and treatment procedures and the complex physiological status of patients in the acute phase. Therefore, this study could not capture the dynamic changes of the TyG index during the acute phase, representing an important limitation. Future studies should consider dynamic monitoring during the acute phase to better characterize these changes and their clinical implications. Follow-up timing and attrition bias The follow-up time points for measuring the TyG index (3, 6, 9, and 12 months) were primarily based on routine clinical schedules, aiming for a preliminary exploration of dynamic changes. However, these time points lacked systematic, evidence-based justification, which may limit a comprehensive understanding of TyG dynamic patterns. Additionally, some patients were lost to follow-up, potentially introducing attrition bias and affecting result reliability. Future multicenter, large-sample studies should design more rigorous follow-up protocols and minimize loss to follow-up to better capture the clinical significance of TyG changes. Lack of separate analysis of fasting glucose and triglyceride trajectories While this study analyzed the TyG index as a composite marker reflecting combined changes in fasting glucose and triglycerides, it did not separately evaluate their independent trajectories. This limits the ability to detail their individual contributions to prognosis and mechanistic understanding. Future studies should incorporate simultaneous dynamic monitoring of both fasting glucose and triglycerides to elucidate the biological mechanisms underlying TyG changes and their association with cardiovascular outcomes. Lack of separate analysis of fasting glucose and triglyceride trajectories While this study analyzed the TyG index as a composite marker reflecting combined changes in fasting glucose and triglycerides, it did not separately evaluate their independent trajectories. This limits the ability to detail their individual contributions to prognosis and mechanistic understanding. Future studies should incorporate simultaneous dynamic monitoring of both fasting glucose and triglycerides to elucidate the biological mechanisms underlying TyG changes and their association with cardiovascular outcomes. Absence of comparison with other insulin resistance markers Due to lack of insulin level data, this study could not compare the TyG index with other insulin resistance markers such as the homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). Although previous studies suggest that the TyG index may outperform HOMA-IR in predicting cardiovascular events, this limitation should be considered when interpreting the results. Future research should include insulin measurements to evaluate the comparative predictive value of different markers. Conclusion This study demonstrated a significant association between the TyG index trajectory and the occurrence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Patients in the “persistently elevated” trajectory group exhibited a worse prognosis and a significantly increased risk of MACE. For this high-risk population, more proactive metabolic management and cardiovascular protection strategies should be considered to reduce the incidence of adverse events and improve long-term clinical outcomes. Research insights What is currently known about this topic? The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index is a validated surrogate marker of insulin resistance and is associated with cardiovascular risk. Most previous studies have relied on single-timepoint measurements of the TyG index, which may not capture its dynamic metabolic changes. Dynamic metabolic markers may provide better prognostic information than static measurements. What is the key research question? How do longitudinal trajectories of the TyG index after PCI in STEMI patients affect their long-term cardiovascular outcomes? What is new? Using group-based trajectory modeling, three distinct TyG trajectories—persistently high, moderate, and rapidly declining—were identified in a large STEMI cohort. Patients with a rapid decline in TyG index had significantly lower rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). TyG trajectory was found to be an independent predictor of long-term prognosis. How might this study influence clinical practice? Dynamic monitoring of TyG trajectories may enable improved risk stratification and personalized secondary prevention in STEMI patients.

chunks.content: 1 Introduction The number of critically ill patients with coronary artery disease undergoing high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) supported by mechanical circulatory support (MCS) devices such as the microaxial flow-pump Impella (Abiomed by J&J, Danvers, Massachusetts) has steadily increased over the past decade. The relevance of this topic was underscored by the recent DanGer Shock trial, which showed a mortality reduction when Impella support was added to standard care in STEMI patients with cardiogenic shock. PCI mandates dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with acetylsalicylic acid and an oral P2Y 12 inhibitor (P2Y 12 i) to prevent ischemic complications, including early stent thrombosis. However, this benefit is offset by an increased risk of bleeding. Managing antiplatelet therapy in critically ill patients is particularly challenging: the efficacy of oral P2Y 12 i may be compromised by impaired gastrointestinal absorption and hepatic metabolism in the setting of hemodynamic instability and organ hypoperfusion. Moreover, Impella support itself increases bleeding risk through thrombocytopenia and proteolysis of von Willebrand factor. Cangrelor, an intravenous P2Y 12 i, provides rapid, potent, and quickly reversible platelet inhibition, making it an attractive option for critically ill PCI patients at high ischemic and bleeding risk. Beyond its pharmacokinetic advantages, recent studies have further clarified both the strengths and limitations of cangrelor in real–world PCI. While it ensures immediate platelet suppression during PCI, variability in platelet reactivity may occur during transition to oral agents, depending on timing and the choice of oral P2Y 12 i. Pharmacodynamic comparisons also suggest that glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors may achieve even more potent early platelet inhibition than cangrelor, underscoring the need to individualize intravenous antiplatelet strategies. . Two randomized clinical trials have demonstrated potential advantages of cangrelor over selected oral P2Y 12 i. , In CHAMPION–PHOENIX, cangrelor significantly reduced the primary ischemic composite endpoint compared with clopidogrel. In DAPT–SHOCK–AMI, cangrelor reduced the secondary ischemic composite endpoint compared with ticagrelor, although the primary endpoint was not met. Despite these findings, evidence supporting cangrelor use in patients undergoing PCI with mechanical circulatory support remains limited. , In this context, we compared outcomes of DAPT with oral P2Y 12 i alone versus cangrelor loading among real-world patient cohort requiring Impella–supported PCI. 2 Methods 2.1 Study setting and population We analyzed data from consecutive patients enrolled in an observational mechanical circulatory support (MCS) device registry ( NCT04117230 ) at the Heart Center of the Luzerner Kantonsspital, Luzern, Switzerland, which serves as the tertiary cardiology facility for the central region of Switzerland. Between 2015 and 2019, data were collected retrospectively, and from August 2019 onward, data were collected prospectively. We included virtually all patients who underwent protected or urgent PCI supported by an Impella microaxial flow pump (Abiomed by J&J, Danvers, MA) at our institution between 2015 and 2025. Exclusion criteria were age < 18 years or refusal of consent. For the current analysis, we additionally excluded patients presenting with cardiogenic shock requiring MCS due to non–ischemic causes (e.g., Takotsubo syndrome, cardiac arrhythmia, valvular heart disease, acute heart failure, or acute myocarditis). 2.2 Data collection and event adjudication Data was collected by trained study personnel and entered into an electronic database (REDCap, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN). Information included demographics, medical history, cardiovascular risk factors, indication for hospital admission and device implantation, procedural characteristics, periprocedural antithrombotic regimen, periprocedural complications within 48h, in-hospital outcomes, and 6-month clinical events. Follow-up data were obtained through scheduled outpatient visits or by structured telephone interviews. In addition, institutional electronic medical records and reports from out-patient cardiologists or other specialists were systematically reviewed. When follow-up information was incomplete or missing, patients’ relatives or referring physicians were contacted by telephone to ascertain the occurrence of any post-discharge events. If a potential event was identified, relevant source documents (e.g., hospital reports, procedural reports, or imaging findings) were retrieved. Each follow-up event was documented in a dedicated follow-up event record and adjudicated accordingly. All study outcomes were adjudicated by two independent investigators (experienced physicians) who were not involved in the clinical management of the patients. Any discrepancies were resolved by consensus with a senior investigator. 2.3 Outcomes of interest The objective was to compare the incidence of periprocedural complications within 48h, in-hospital outcomes as well as 6-month clinical events between patients undergoing Impella-supported PCI treated with DAPT using oral P2Y 12 i only versus loading with cangrelor followed by oral P2Y 12 i. Periprocedural complications within 48 h included: angiographically confirmed myocardial re-infarction, hemodynamically relevant pericardial effusion, resuscitation unrelated to underlying deterioration, and bleeding events classified as minor (BARC < 3) or major (BARC ≥ 3). Bleeding was further categorized by Bleeding Academic Research Consortium stage (BARC 1–5) and by type (device puncture site, angiography access site, venous access site, intracranial, pericardial, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, epistaxis, enoral, urogenital, hemothorax, and other). . In-hospital outcomes included: mean intermediate care unit (ICU) length of stay, transfusion

Periprocedural complications within 48 h included: angiographically confirmed myocardial re-infarction, hemodynamically relevant pericardial effusion, resuscitation unrelated to underlying deterioration, and bleeding events classified as minor (BARC < 3) or major (BARC ≥ 3). Bleeding was further categorized by Bleeding Academic Research Consortium stage (BARC 1–5) and by type (device puncture site, angiography access site, venous access site, intracranial, pericardial, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, epistaxis, enoral, urogenital, hemothorax, and other). . In-hospital outcomes included: mean intermediate care unit (ICU) length of stay, transfusion requirements (packed red blood cells and platelet concentrates), early stent thrombosis, target lesion revascularization (TLR), target vessel revascularization, revascularization of another vessel, recurrent MI, ischemic or hemorrhagic cerebrovascular insult (CVI), coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), all-cause mortality, cardiovascular (CV) mortality, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). MACE was defined as a composite of recurrent MI, CVI, and CV mortality. 6-month clinical events included MI, CVI, repeat PCI, TLR, all-cause mortality, CV mortality and MACE. The primary outcomes comprised periprocedural major bleeding (BARC ≥ 3) within 48h, in-hospital MACE and 6-month MACE. 2.4 Antithrombotic management Our local practice generally follows contemporaneous international guideline recommendations for the management of acute and chronic coronary disease. , , , , , , , , , , , , Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) consisted of aspirin plus a loading dose of a P2Y 12 i, administered either orally (clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor) or intravenously as cangrelor, followed by maintenance therapy. The choice of antiplatelet regimen in each case was left to the treating physician and was influenced by the patient’s clinical condition, age, comorbidities, and the estimated ischemic and bleeding risk. Over the study period, a temporal shift in P2Y 12 i selection was observed in patients with acute coronary syndromes, with decreasing use of clopidogrel and increasing use of the more potent agents prasugrel and ticagrelor . For cangrelor administration, we followed the manufacturer’s instructions for use. Patients treated with cangrelor received a 30 µg/kg bolus followed by a continuous infusion of 4 µg/kg/min, according to the CHAMPION‑PLATFORM study protocol After the PCI procedure and once clinical stabilization was achieved, patients treated with cangrelor were transitioned to an oral P2Y 12 i Patients on cangrelor received a loading dose of ticagrelor (180 mg) and the cangrelor infusion was continued for at least 30 min. For patients not eligible for ticagrelor loading, a loading dose of clopidogrel (600 mg) was given and the cangrelor infusion was discontinued. In our practice, for patients receiving oral P2Y12 inhibitor loading only, we generally administer the loading dose of the preferred agent—ticagrelor, prasugrel, or clopidogrel—once the coronary anatomy and PCI strategy have been defined directly in the catheterization laboratory during the PCI procedure. Treatment with oral P2Y 12 i is typically continued for 6–12 months. All patients received unfractionated heparin during PCI to maintain an activated clotting time (ACT) > 250 s. 2.5 Implantation and management of microaxial flow pump The Impella microaxial flow pump was implanted fully percutaneously via the femoral artery using 12 Fr (Impella 2.5) or 14 Fr (CP) sheaths. Ultrasound guidance was used if possible. Whenever feasible, a single-access–only strategy was adopted, using the same femoral arterial access for both Impella implantation and PCI in order to minimize additional vascular punctures. The device was inserted over a stiff 0.018-inch guidewire, advanced under fluoroscopy, and positioned retrogradely across the aortic valve. Impella was explanted as soon as clinically feasible based on the patient’s hemodynamic status. 2.6 PCI procedures For PCI procedures at our institution, all interventions were performed in accordance with current international guideline recommendations. , Lesion preparation was typically achieved using pre-dilatation with semi- or non-compliant balloons. Additional devices such as modified balloons, atherectomy, or intravascular lithotripsy were used when indicated. Latest-generation drug-eluting stents were routinely implanted. Direct stenting was reserved for selected cases, while thrombectomy was performed as a bailout strategy or for large thrombus burden (TIMI 4–5). Institutional standards encouraged liberal use of intravascular imaging for lesion characterization and/or stent optimization. Post-dilatation was generally performed with appropriately sized non-compliant balloons at high pressure (>18 atm) to ensure optimal stent expansion and apposition. 2.7 Statistical analysis Categorical data are reported as frequencies and percentages, whereas continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviations when distributions were not heavily skewed or when the mean was considered more informative, and as median with interquartile range when skewed with extreme outliers. Statistical comparisons were conducted using Pearson's chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and either Student's t -test, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, or the Wilcoxon exact test for continuous variables, depending on distributional assumptions and sample size. Cumulative incidence of clinical outcomes was estimated with 95% confidence intervals and compared using Gray's test.

Statistical analysis Categorical data are reported as frequencies and percentages, whereas continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviations when distributions were not heavily skewed or when the mean was considered more informative, and as median with interquartile range when skewed with extreme outliers. Statistical comparisons were conducted using Pearson's chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and either Student's t -test, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, or the Wilcoxon exact test for continuous variables, depending on distributional assumptions and sample size. Cumulative incidence of clinical outcomes was estimated with 95% confidence intervals and compared using Gray's test. Predictors of MACE were analysed with Cox proportional hazards models, and predictors of major bleeding (BARC ≥ 3) within 48 h of the index procedure with logistic regression; results are reported as hazard ratios or odds ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals and p-values. To address confounding by indication, propensity scores for receiving cangrelor were estimated using logistic regression including clinically relevant baseline characteristics associated with treatment allocation (cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, STEMI, elective high-risk protected PCI, age, and sex). Stabilised inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) were computed to estimate the average treatment effect. Covariate balance was assessed using absolute standardised mean differences (threshold < 0.1). IPTW-adjusted treatment effects were estimated using weighted logistic regression with robust standard errors for binary outcomes and weighted Cox regression with robust variance for 6-month MACE; the proportional hazards assumption was verified using Schoenfeld residuals. Sensitivity analyses included weight trimming at the 99th percentile, average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) estimation, and an expanded propensity score model additionally including left ventricular ejection fraction and SCAI shock stage. Exploratory subgroup analyses assessed whether treatment effects differed by cardiogenic shock status, STEMI presentation, and age (above/below the median). Within each stratum, binary outcomes were compared using Fisher's exact test and logistic regression, while 6-month MACE was compared using the log-rank test and Cox regression. Treatment-by-subgroup interaction was tested using Wald tests for the interaction term in pooled models. No correction for multiple testing was applied. Events-per-variable (EPV) ratios and effective sample sizes after IPTW weighting were calculated for all multivariable models to assess model adequacy. A two-tailed p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Descriptive analyses and regression models were performed using R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024). IPTW, subgroup analyses, and model diagnostics were performed using Python 3.12 (pandas, statsmodels, lifelines). 2.8 Ethics Data collection and analysis were approved by the regional ethics board (BASEC ID: 201,901,067 and 201900274). Participants were informed about the observational nature of the study, including clinical or telephone follow-ups, and written consent was obtained whenever possible. If a patient’s medical condition precluded informed consent, consent was obtained from a legally authorized representative. A waiver of consent was granted for patients unable to provide consent before or after the intervention due to the severity of their condition or death. All patient data were anonymized prior to analysis. 3 Results 3.1 Patients’ characteristics Overall, 295 consecutive patients undergoing Impella-supported PCI were enrolled. Of these, 201 received oral P2Y 12 i only and 94 received loading with cangrelor followed by an oral P2Y 12 i, see . Baseline characteristics are summarized in . The mean age of the cohort was 67.8 ± 11.1 years, with no significant difference between groups (68.3 ± 11.2 years versus 66.7 ± 11.0 years). Although not statistically significant, patients treated with oral P2Y 12 i more frequently had history of hypertension (63% versus 55%), dyslipidemia (54% versus 45%), previous MI (22% versus 16%), previous PCI (27% versus 20%), and previous CABG (6.5% versus 2.1%) compared with those receiving cangrelor loading. At admission, patients in the oral P2Y 12 i group presented less often with cardiac arrest (18.9% versus 31.9%, p = 0.013) and cardiogenic shock (55.2% versus 72.3%, p = 0.005) but were more frequently admitted for high-risk protected PCI (17.9% versus 6.4%, p = 0.008). High-risk protected PCI was defined as elective Impella placement before PCI to enhance safety in patients with unprotected left main coronary artery disease, last remaining vessel intervention, left ventricular ejection fraction < 35%, complex three-vessel disease or significant comorbidities including severe aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation. 3.2 Periprocedural antithrombotic treatment and procedural characteristics Almost all patients received aspirin and unfractionated heparin before PCI. Ticagrelor was the most frequently used oral P2Y 12 i in both groups (80.1% versus 90.4%). Clopidogrel use was higher in the oral P2Y 12 i group than in the cangrelor group (19.9% versus 4.3%) ( Table S1) . Clopidogrel use was higher in the oral P2Y 12 i group than in the cangrelor group (19.9% versus 4.3%) ( Table S1) . Femoral access (71.9%) was used more often than radial (28.1%), with similar distribution between groups. Impella devices were generally implanted before PCI (68.7% versus 59.6%) and rarely after (11.4% versus 11.7%). The type of MCS device differed significantly. Impella 2.5 was used only in the oral P2Y 12 i group (5.5% versus 0.0%), whereas Impella CP predominated in both groups (94.5% versus 98.9%). When an additional MCS device was required, IABP was more common in the oral P2Y 12 i group (10.0% versus 2.1%), whereas VA-ECMO was more frequent in the cangrelor group (2.5% versus 4.3%). Left anterior descending artery (LAD) was the most commonly treated vessel (74.6% versus 72.3%). Pre-PCI TIMI flow was mostly TIMI 0 (39.3% versus 60.6%), while post-PCI TIMI 3 flow was achieved in most cases (91.5% versus 85.1%). True bifurcation culprit lesions were more frequent in the oral P2Y 12 i group (34.9% versus 20.2%) and were mostly treated with both-branch stenting (22.4% versus 8.5%). The use of rotablation or shockwave lithotripsy (8.5% versus 10.6%) and chronic total occlusion (CTO) treatment (6.5% versus 4.3%) was not statistically different between groups. The number of vessels (1.5 ± 0.6 versus 1.2 ± 0.4) and lesions (2.5 ± 1.5 versus 1.9 ± 1.3) treated, as well as the number of stents implanted (2.3 ± 1.6 versus 1.7 ± 1.3), were significantly higher in the oral P2Y 12 i group. Successful revascularization was high in both groups (91.6% versus 94.7%). Of note, the Impella-support time did not significantly differ between the two groups. 3.3 Periprocedural complications within 48 h and in-hospital outcomes Most periprocedural complications within 48 h were not statistically different between groups ( ) ; new onset of MI (0.5% versus 1.1%) and need of resuscitation (3.0% versus 6.4%). Hemorrhagic pericardial effusion occurred significantly less often in the oral P2Y 12 i group (0.0% versus 3.2%). Major bleeding (BARC ≥ 3) within 48 h post-PCI was insignificantly higher in the cangrelor group (26.4% versus 33.0%, p = 0.2), while rates of minor bleeding were similar (33.8% versus 35.1%) between both groups. No significant differences were observed for in-hospital outcomes ( ) : The mean ICU stay length was slightly shorter in the oral P2Y 12 i group (6.1 ± 9.0 days versus 6.9 ± 11.1 days). Red blood cell transfusion requirements (1.7 ± 3.4 versus 1.9 ± 3.6) were marginally lower in the oral P2Y 12 i group. Early stent thrombosis occurred in 2 patients in each group (1.0% versus 2.1%) and TLR was similarly infrequent (1.5% versus 1.1%). Rates of in-hospital MI (2.0% versus 2.1%) and CVI (3.5% versus 5.3%) were comparable. CABG during index hospitalization was more frequently indicated in the cangrelor group (0.5% versus 3.2%). All-cause mortality (21.9% versus 26.6%) was slightly higher in the cangrelor group, while cardiovascular mortality was similar (18.4% versus 18.1%). MACE rates were comparable between groups (23.9% versus 24.5%). 3.4 Periprocedural minor and major bleedings within 48 h Overall, the rate of any bleeding was high. Out of 101 patients with minor bleeding within 48 h post-PCI, 99 (98.0%) were classified as BARC 2. Most common cause of minor bleeding were bleedings from the device puncture site (81.2%). There were no significant differences between the groups in terms of type of bleeding (Table S2) . The major bleeding events are summarized in Table S3 . Out of 84 patients with major bleeding within 48 h post-PCI, 63 (75.0%) were classified as BARC 3a. Most common cause of major bleeding were bleedings from the device puncture site (75.0%). Among all major bleeding events, those related to the device puncture site were significantly more frequent in the oral P2Y 12 i group (88.7%) compared to the cangrelor group (51.6%). 3.5 6-month clinical events and Fig. S1 show 6-month clinical events. At 6 months, all-cause mortality occurred in 50 patients in the oral P2Y 12 i group and 33 in the cangrelor group, corresponding to cumulative incidences of 25% and 35%, respectively. The mortality curves separated within the first 30 days and remained divergent thereafter. CV mortality accounted for most deaths in both groups. At 6 months, it occurred in 40 patients in the oral P2Y 12 i group compared with 24 patients in the cangrelor group, with cumulative incidences of 21% versus 27%, respectively. At 6 months, 54 MACE events occurred in the oral P2Y 12 i group and 31 in the cangrelor group, with cumulative incidences of 28% versus 35%, respectively. Most events occurred within the first 45 days in both groups. 3.6 Predictors for major bleeding (BARC ≥ 3) and MACE In univariable analysis, admission with cardiogenic shock was the strongest predictor of major bleeding (BARC ≥ 3) within 48 h post-PCI (OR 3.48, 95% CI 1.96–6.49), while female sex was also associated with increased bleeding risk (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.06–3.58) ( ) . In multivariable analysis, cardiogenic shock remained significantly associated with major bleeding (OR 7.09, 95% CI 2.97–18.49). No other baseline comorbidities or clinical presentations were independently associated. For MACE at 6 months ( ) , age was the only significant predictor in univariable analysis (HR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01–1.05). In multivariable analysis, age (HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.02–1.06) and cardiogenic shock on admission (HR 2.01, 95% CI 1.01–3.97) remained independently associated with MACE. Other variables, including previous renal failure, previous peripheral artery disease, previous diabetes, and presentation with STEMI or NSTEMI, were not significantly associated with outcomes in adjusted analyses. 3.7 Propensity score-adjusted treatment effects The propensity score model achieved excellent covariate balance after inverse probability of treatment weighting (Fig. S2A) . All absolute standardized mean differences were reduced below 0.05, from a maximum of 0.36 for cardiogenic shock before weighting. Propensity score distributions showed substantial overlap between treatment groups (Fig. S2B) , with effective sample sizes of 82.2 for cangrelor (of 94) and 197.2 for oral P2Y 12 i (of 201). After IPTW adjustment, no significant differences were observed between cangrelor and oral P2Y 12 i for any of the three primary outcomes: major bleeding BARC ≥ 3 within 48 h (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.58–1.73, p = 1.00), in-hospital MACE (OR 1.06, 95% CI 0.61–1.85, p = 0.84), and 6-month MACE (HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.65–1.75, p = 0.80) (Table S4) . Sensitivity analyses using trimmed weights, ATT estimation, and an expanded propensity score model including left ventricular ejection fraction and SCAI shock stage yielded concordant results (Table S4) . 3.8 Subgroup analyses Exploratory subgroup analyses revealed a significant interaction between cardiogenic shock status and treatment effect on ischaemic outcomes (Table S5, Fig. S3) . Among patients with cardiogenic shock (n = 179), cangrelor was associated with a non-significant trend towards lower MACE rates compared with oral P2Y 12 i, both in-hospital (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.30–1.25, p = 0.22) and at 6 months (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.37–1.25, p = 0.21). Conversely, among patients without cardiogenic shock (n = 116), cangrelor was associated with higher MACE rates (in-hospital: OR 2.65, 95% CI 0.99–7.05, p = 0.06; 6-month: HR 2.33, 95% CI 1.07–5.10, p = 0.03). Formal interaction tests were significant for both in-hospital MACE (p = 0.02) and 6-month MACE (p = 0.02). A similar pattern was observed when stratifying by STEMI presentation (interaction p = 0.003 for both MACE outcomes), although 85% of patients with cardiogenic shock also presented with STEMI, limiting the independence of these findings. No significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction was observed for major bleeding (all interaction p > 0.5) or when stratifying by age (all interaction p > 0.2). 4 Discussion Cangrelor is increasingly used in critically ill and complex patients undergoing PCI, yet evidence regarding its safety and efficacy in the setting of MCS remains limited. In this well-characterized cohort, we provide one of the first analyses evaluating intravenous P2Y 12 i cangrelor during PCI supported by a microaxial flow pump. The three principal findings were: (i) bleeding risk in this context is very high, but the use of cangrelor compared with oral P2Y 12 i does not seem to alter the risk of bleeding; (ii) cangrelor administration during Impella-supported PCI did not alter ischemic complications, including stent thrombosis, recurrent MI and CVI; and (iii) in-hospital mortality was not statistically different between both groups. analyses evaluating intravenous P2Y 12 i cangrelor during PCI supported by a microaxial flow pump. The three principal findings were: (i) bleeding risk in this context is very high, but the use of cangrelor compared with oral P2Y 12 i does not seem to alter the risk of bleeding; (ii) cangrelor administration during Impella-supported PCI did not alter ischemic complications, including stent thrombosis, recurrent MI and CVI; and (iii) in-hospital mortality was not statistically different between both groups. Although the findings remained consistent after adjustment for baseline differences, supporting the robustness of the observed neutral treatment effect, they should be interpreted with caution given the observational design, non-random treatment allocation, and potential residual confounding. Accordingly, these results are descriptive and hypothesis-generating and do not permit causal inference regarding the comparative effects of cangrelor and oral P2Y 12 i in Impella-supported PCI. During the study period, clinical practice evolved, with increasing use of Impella in cardiogenic shock and a shift toward more potent oral P2Y 12 i. These temporal changes may have introduced bias and should be considered when interpreting the findings. In routine practice, cangrelor was preferentially used in more unstable patients, including those with cardiac arrest and advanced SCAI shock stages, often requiring prolonged support and delayed transition to oral therapy. In contrast, oral P2Y 12 i were more frequently used in elective high-risk PCI with greater procedural complexity but shorter device support. These differences suggest that the groups represent distinct clinical populations. Importantly, IPTW achieved excellent covariate balance, and adjusted analyses confirmed the absence of statistically significant differences in bleeding and MACE. While residual confounding cannot be excluded, these findings suggest that measured baseline differences are unlikely to account for the neutral results. Exploratory subgroup analyses revealed a significant interaction between treatment and cardiogenic shock for ischemic outcomes. Cangrelor showed a non-significant trend toward lower MACE in shock patients, whereas the opposite pattern was observed in patients without shock. This suggests that the clinical impact of intravenous platelet inhibition may depend on hemodynamic status. In cardiogenic shock, impaired absorption and high thrombotic burden may limit oral P2Y 12 i efficacy, potentially favoring intravenous strategies. In more stable patients, however, additional platelet inhibition may not confer benefit. These findings are exploratory, not adjusted for multiplicity, and confounded by overlap with STEMI, and should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating. Bleeding and thrombotic event rates were high and reflect the severity of illness and procedural complexity rather than the antiplatelet strategy alone. , , , , Bleeding was affected by access-site complications in the context of large-bore femoral access, mechanical support, and critical illness. Thrombotic risk was influenced by hemodynamic instability, high thrombus burden, and impaired drug absorption. Although a single femoral access strategy was used whenever feasible to limit vascular complications, femoral large-bore access remains an inherent limitation of Impella-supported PCI and may have contributed to bleeding events. In addition, hemodilution from aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation in critically ill patients may have contributed to higher hemoglobin declines in patients with bleeding meeting BARC 3a criteria. Although cardiogenic shock was a strong predictor of post-PCI bleeding, cangrelor-treated patients did not exhibit higher bleeding rates despite a greater prevalence of shock, with comparable ischemic outcomes between treatment groups. While oral P2Y 12 i remain the standard of care and cangrelor carries a Class IIb recommendation in P2Y 12 i–naïve patients undergoing PCI. , , Cangrelor’s intravenous administration, rapid reversibility due to short half-life and absence of cytochrome P450-mediated drug interactions may be advantageous in selected Impella-supported PCI, where thrombosis and bleeding risk coexist. , Registry and pharmacodynamic data suggest that cangrelor provides effective intraprocedural platelet inhibition, but its clinical impact may depend substantially on transition to oral therapy. , In addition, the substantially higher cost of cangrelor compared with generic oral P2Y 12 i may limit broader adoption. Alternative intravenous strategies, such as glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors, may offer even more potent immediate platelet inhibition, although their bleeding profiles require careful consideration, particularly in patients with large-bore vascular access and mechanical circulatory support. . Overall, the evidence informing antiplatelet therapy during PCI with MCS remains limited and heterogeneous. Randomized cangrelor trials largely excluded patients with MCS or cardiogenic shock. , , Observational studies and registry data in shock and MCS populations have reported mixed findings, with inconsistent signals for ischemic benefit and bleeding risk. , , , , , , , , , , , , , Most recently, DAPT-SHOCK-AMI suggested potential ischemic benefit with cangrelor, but uncertainty remains. , Taken together, these data underscore the need for adequately powered studies to define the optimal antiplatelet strategy in this setting. 6-month outcomes were reported according to the initially selected antiplatelet strategy. registry data in shock and MCS populations have reported mixed findings, with inconsistent signals for ischemic benefit and bleeding risk. , , , , , , , , , , , , , Most recently, DAPT-SHOCK-AMI suggested potential ischemic benefit with cangrelor, but uncertainty remains. , Taken together, these data underscore the need for adequately powered studies to define the optimal antiplatelet strategy in this setting. 6-month outcomes were reported according to the initially selected antiplatelet strategy. However, these data should be interpreted cautiously. As cangrelor was administered only periprocedurally and both groups received oral therapy thereafter, long-term outcomes cannot be attributed to initial treatment strategy and likely reflect baseline risk differences. Therefore, 6-month outcomes should not be interpreted as reflecting a treatment effect of cangrelor but rather underlying baseline risk. Taken together, these findings suggest that in Impella-supported PCI, clinical outcomes are driven more by illness severity, particularly cardiogenic shock, and procedural complexity than by the choice of antiplatelet strategy. We acknowledge several limitations. First, this is a single-center observational analysis, which limits generalizability and precludes causal inference. Treatment allocation was non-random and influenced by clinical severity, resulting in confounding by indication. Although inverse probability of treatment weighting achieved excellent balance in measured covariates, residual confounding from unmeasured factors cannot be excluded, and the propensity score model was limited to available variables. Second, the relatively small sample size and number of events limited statistical power and the complexity of multivariable modeling. Events-per-variable (EPV) ratios in the fully adjusted models were below recommended thresholds, indicating a potential risk of overfitting. However, results were consistent in reduced models and in IPTW-based analyses with substantially higher EPV ratios, supporting the overall robustness of the findings. Third, subgroup analyses were exploratory, not pre-specified, and multiple interaction tests were performed without adjustment for multiplicity. In addition, substantial overlap between cardiogenic shock and STEMI limits the independence of subgroup findings. These results should therefore be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. Fourth, the study spanned a 10-year period during which PCI techniques, patient selection for Impella support, antithrombotic strategies, and overall management of cardiogenic shock evolved substantially. These temporal changes may have influenced both treatment allocation and clinical outcomes, introducing potential temporal confounding. Because of the limited sample size and number of outcome events, we were unable to perform robust era-adjusted sensitivity analyses. Finally, heterogeneity in antiplatelet strategies, including the use of different oral P2Y 12 i, variability in cangrelor infusion duration, and differences in Impella support time, was not fully captured and may have influenced both bleeding and ischemic outcomes. 5 Conclusions In this real-world cohort of patients undergoing Impella-supported PCI, cangrelor was associated with similar bleeding and ischemic outcomes compared with oral P2Y 12 i, despite higher clinical acuity in the cangrelor group. These findings remained consistent after adjustment for baseline differences using propensity score weighting, supporting the robustness of the overall neutral treatment effect. However, interpretation is limited by the observational design and modest statistical power. Exploratory analyses suggest that treatment effects may differ according to clinical presentation, particularly in patients with cardiogenic shock. Accordingly, antiplatelet therapy in Impella-supported PCI should be individualized, and adequately powered randomized trials are needed to define the optimal strategy in this high-risk population. 6 Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process During the preparation of this work, the authors used ChatGPT (OpenAI, San Francisco, CA, USA) to assist with language refinement and improvement of scientific phrasing. chunks.content: Introduction Background Coronary artery disease (CAD) is one of the leading causes of hospitalization and mortality worldwide, with older adults aged 60 years and older being the most affected [ ]. Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is the gold standard treatment for severe CAD and has been shown to improve survival, quality of life, and long-term cardiovascular outcomes by reducing recurrent myocardial infarction and the need for repeat revascularization [ ]. This is particularly important given the increasing number of older patients requiring CABG, many of whom have multiple comorbidities, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and renal disease, which are common in older adults and require complex clinical management. Despite advancements in CABG, it remains highly stressful and traumatic for patients [ ]. Older individuals undergoing CABG face many preoperative and postoperative physical and psychological challenges, which may adversely affect recovery and increase the risk of rehospitalization [ ]. In Thailand, more than 6000 CABG procedures are performed annually [ ], and most patients are older adults with preexisting comorbidities [ ]. Rehospitalization within 28 days after discharge occurs in approximately 15.6% of patients and is commonly attributed to wound infections, fatigue, chest pain, and syncope [ ]. Functional status is a key indicator of recovery after CABG, particularly in older patients. Older patients who underwent CABG have been reported to be particularly susceptible to decline in activities of daily living after surgery compared with their younger counterparts [ ] and experience a slow recovery in functional status following surgery [ ]. Psychological factors, particularly anxiety and depression, significantly influence recovery following CABG and are associated with delayed recovery, higher readmission rates, and increased mortality, especially in older adults [ ]. These symptoms may persist or worsen after surgery due to the stress of surgery [ ]. Preoperative anxiety and depression have been associated with higher mortality and poorer postoperative outcomes. Older patients undergoing CABG tend to experience higher levels of these symptoms than younger patients [ ]. Inadequate postoperative care and ineffective communication may exacerbate psychological distress, resulting in poor care transitions and adverse outcomes [ ]. System-level challenges, including workforce shortages, fragmented communication, and insufficient continuity of care, further contribute to care transition failures, increased adverse events, and higher rehospitalization rates [ ]. Consequently, older adults with complex health conditions undergoing CABG are particularly vulnerable to poor postoperative outcomes. Various programs, including standard discharge planning, cardiac rehabilitation, and patient education, are recommended to improve recovery and reduce rehospitalization after CABG [ ]. Furthermore, nurses play a crucial role in guiding patients undergoing CABG and their family caregivers throughout the recovery process. However, usual care tends to be hospital-centered, with limited focus on home-based monitoring and postdischarge counseling. Telehealth Telehealth has emerged as an important strategy for postdischarge management after CABG, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. Telehealth interventions have been shown to enhance patient engagement and satisfaction, support symptom monitoring, and enable timely clinical responses, thereby promoting continuity of care and reducing rehospitalization [ ]. These interventions, including video consultations, remote monitoring, and educational platforms, also contribute to improvements in physical and psychological recovery. Telehealth interventions, particularly those incorporating mobile health apps, have shown promise in improving functional health outcomes in older patients with cardiac conditions through cardiac rehabilitation and home monitoring [ ]. Furthermore, telehealth, based on the transitional care model (TCM) integrating with remote monitoring and scheduled video visits, has also improved medication adherence, self-care, and rehospitalization outcomes in patients with chronic cardiovascular conditions [ ]. However, most telehealth studies have been conducted in developed countries using diverse technologies and methods [ ]. In Asia, telehealth has been applied to rehabilitation for long COVID-19 and home-based exercise among patients with cardiometabolic multimorbidity [ ]. Nevertheless, evidence specific to older patients undergoing CABG remains limited, and prior studies in Thailand have largely focused on rehabilitation and monitoring, with less emphasis on psychological outcomes and postdischarge consultation [ ]. Barriers to telehealth adoption among older adults include technological limitations and physical impairments [ ]. Conversely, individualized approaches, patient-centered education, and age-friendly design features can enhance user satisfaction and engagement [ ]. Furthermore, family and social support are critical for successful implementation of telehealth [ ]. This study incorporated family caregivers into the telehealth intervention to address these challenges, enabling them to assist older patients undergoing CABG with daily activities and care management during the postdischarge period. Therefore, the study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of telehealth intervention in improving functional status, anxiety, depression, and rehospitalization compared with usual care among older patients undergoing CABG. Methods Overview This study used a 2-arm, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial with a pretest-posttest control group design and repeated measures. Participants were randomly assigned to either the intervention or control group using a 1:1 block randomization method. The care protocols for each group are outlined below. Description of the Intervention The intervention group received the telehealth intervention in addition to usual care. The telehealth intervention protocol was guided by the TCM [ ] ( ). The telehealth intervention was conducted by a researcher who was a specialist cardiac nurse with at least 5 years of experience in cardiac care. The care process started in the hospital and continued to the participants’ homes based on the eight core TCM components: (1) screening, (2) engaging the older adults and caregiver, (3) managing symptoms, (4) educating and promoting self-management, (5) collaboration, (6) assuring continuity, (7) coordinating care, and (8) maintaining relationships. The telehealth intervention encompassed 2 phases of the care process. Phase 1 involved discharge planning at the cardiac surgical units. During hospitalization, the researcher developed individualized care plans, provided health education through a booklet, and trained participants and caregivers in self-management and the use of the “Zip Heart” app. Vital signs (eg, heart rate and blood pressure) were measured using automated devices and manually entered into the app by participants or caregivers. Devices and internet access were provided as needed, and follow-up video calls were scheduled prior to discharge. Phase 2 involved home monitoring via the “Zip Heart” app and video call visits, providing continuous postdischarge support and monitoring in the home setting. In the first month, the participants used the “Zip Heart” app to record their vital signs. They also received daily reminders and weekly video calls addressing symptoms, activities, and concerns, starting in the first week after discharge. Each call lasted 10‐20 minutes, depending on the participant’s recovery progress [ ]. Video calls also enabled visual assessment of the participant’s physical condition and environment. The researcher consulted with a multidisciplinary team to address specific needs. All relevant data were recorded in the integrated discharge planning screening and follow-up form. Furthermore, infographics on postoperative care and cardiac rehabilitation were shared weekly. In the second and third months, the participants received biweekly video calls and weekly infographics on secondary cardiac prevention and behavior modification. Although all participants were scheduled for at least 8 video call visits during the study, the researcher used clinical judgment to determine if additional visits were needed. The video call visits ended when the participant was able to resume daily activities and required no further support from the health care team. An interview guide developed for this study was used to minimize respondents’ burden and avoid repetitive questioning. Participants in the intervention group continued to receive routine postoperative outpatient clinic follow-up as part of usual care. A representative telehealth intervention is presented in . Control Group The control group received usual care by the cardiac nurse, including orientation to the surgical unit, health education, and standard discharge planning. Postoperatively, the cardiac nurse and a multidisciplinary team monitored recovery, managed pain, encouraged rehabilitation exercises, and prepared participants and caregivers for discharge. On the day of discharge, participants received standardized discharge instructions based on the D-METHOD framework (Diagnosis, Medications, Environment, Treatment, Health behaviors, Outpatient follow-up, and Diet). This framework included information on diagnosis, medications, home environment, treatment regimen, health behaviors, outpatient follow-up, dietary recommendations, wound care, and potential complications. Participants were advised to attend a follow-up appointment with their cardiac surgeon one week after discharge at the outpatient department (OPD) and were provided with the surgical unit’s contact information for any health-related inquiries [ ]. The corresponding effect size, calculated using Cohen d based on the group means and SDs, was 0.7, indicating a medium effect. Based on this effect size, the required sample size was estimated to be 33 participants per group. To account for anticipated attrition, the sample size was increased to 42 participants per group (84 in total), corresponding to an approximate attrition allowance of 21.4%. Sampling A probability sampling method was used in this study. Participants were randomly selected from patients aged 60 years and older who were admitted for their first elective isolated CABG and met the inclusion criteria. Eligible participants were identified through the hospital’s surgical scheduling system, which served as the sampling frame. Patients were consecutively selected based on their scheduled surgery dates, according to the standard CABG surgical list, until the required sample size was reached. Participant Recruitment and Enrollment All patients admitted for first-time elective isolated CABG were approached by nurses in the Cardiac Surgical Units on the day of hospital admission. These patients were provided with detailed information about the study. Individuals who expressed interest in participating were subsequently assessed by the researcher to determine eligibility based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Eligible individuals were invited to participate and were provided with a participant information sheet. Sufficient time was given to address any questions before obtaining written informed consent. Baseline Assessment After providing written informed consent, all participants were assessed for baseline data by the researcher on the day of hospital admission. The assessments included (1) demographic and clinical characteristics, collected using the Health-Related Data Questionnaire (HRDQ); (2) functional status, measured using the Thai ESDS; and (3) levels of anxiety and depression, assessed using the Thai version of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (Thai HADS). Randomization and Allocation Participants were randomly assigned to the intervention or control group (n=42 per group) using 1:1 block randomization to ensure balanced group sizes. The randomization sequence was generated using a computerized random number generator with a permuted block size of four in Microsoft Excel, with codes “A” (control) and “B” (intervention). Allocation concealment was maintained using sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes prepared according to the randomization sequence. Envelopes were opened only after informed consent was obtained. Participant allocation details, including serial number and patient identification codes, were recorded by the investigator and stored securely. Blinding Design Blinding of treatment allocation was not feasible for either the nurses delivering the intervention or the participants due to the nature of the study design. Therefore, the trial was conducted using an open-label design. To minimize assessment bias, outcome data were collected by a research assistant who was blinded to group allocation, thereby ensuring observer blinding during data collection. However, a residual risk of unblinding remained, as participants may have inadvertently disclosed their group allocation during interviews. Study Design This study was a single-center RCT with a pretest-posttest control group design and repeated measures. The trial evaluated the effectiveness of the telehealth intervention in addition to usual care, compared to usual care only, among older adult patients. This study was conducted in accordance with CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials; checklist provided in ) guidelines for randomized trials involving 2 groups[ ] . Study Setting and Population The study was conducted in 2 phases. Phase 1 took place in the cardiac surgical units of a university hospital in Bangkok, Thailand, between September 2023 and June 2024. Phase 2 involved home-based follow-up assessments at 30 and 90 days after discharge. The target population consisted of older adults undergoing CABG. All patients diagnosed with CAD who were scheduled for elective CABG and met the inclusion criteria were eligible and subsequently enrolled in the study.
